title: Constitution of the Republic of Singapore (Amendment No 3) Bill
what_it_is: Constitution of the Republic of Singapore (Amendment No 3) Bill

sections.label: Cabinet principles for President appointments
sections.summary: Cabinet applies principles on advising the President to take appointments in his official capacity, covering domestic, international, apolitical and constitutional limits.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
sentences.text: In deciding whether to advise the President to take on an appointment in his official capacity, Cabinet applies the following principles: (a)	domestic appointments must be in furtherance of the President’s symbolic and unifying role; (b)	international appointments must be in furtherance of Singapore’s national interest; (c)	the President’s public life must be carried out in a manner that is compatible with his status and role as the Head of State – he is apolitical and cannot become involved in issues or events that might generate political controversy; (d)	in addition, the appointment must not undermine or be incompatible with the President’s discretionary functions under the Constitution, including his custodial functions as the Elected President; (e) the appointment must not contravene Article 19A(1) of the Constitution, which among other things, prohibits the President from being actively engaged in commercial enterprises.

sections.label: Cabinet agrees President continues appointments
sections.summary: Cabinet agreed it is in the national interest for the President to continue these appointments, with no remuneration, though the Attorney-General said the arrangement was not ideal.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
sentences.text: Cabinet has considered the matter and agreed that it is in the national interest for him to continue holding these appointments as President currently in his official capacity.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
sentences.text: And for the information of the House, the President does not receive any remuneration or other benefits from these appointments.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
sentences.text: The Government’s original intention was for President Tharman to continue to serve in these international appointments in his official capacity.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
sentences.text: But after reviewing the matter carefully, we were advised by the Attorney-General that this arrangement was not ideal.

sections.label: President allowed private capacity appointments
sections.summary: Cabinet concluded the President should be allowed to contribute to these international appointments in his independent and private capacity, as this benefits Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
sentences.text: Cabinet considered this carefully and we concluded that the President should be allowed to do so to contribute to these international appointments in his independent and private capacity as this is beneficial for Singapore.

sections.label: Attorney-General says arrangement not provided
sections.summary: The Attorney-General advised that such an arrangement is currently not clearly provided for by the Constitution.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
sentences.text: The Attorney-General, however, advised that such an arrangement is currently not clearly provided for by the Constitution.

sections.label: Article 22Q(1) international appointments conditions
sections.summary: Article 22Q(1) will enable current and future Presidents to accept international appointments in their private capacities, subject to three conditions.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
sentences.text: Article 22Q(1) will enable current and future Presidents to accept international appointments in their private capacities, subject to three conditions.

sections.label: Cabinet advice against certain conduct
sections.summary: As a general rule, Cabinet will advise the President against commenting on domestic politics, laws and policies, making commitments for the Government or Singapore, and retaining remuneration or benefits.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
sentences.text: As a general rule, the Cabinet will advise the President against commenting on domestic politics, laws and policies; making any commitments on behalf of the Government or Singapore, whether formally or informally; and retaining any remuneration or benefits in connection with the appointment.

sections.label: President international appointments consultation rules
sections.summary: The President need not consult the Council of Presidential Advisers and faces no time limit on international appointments, with Article 22Q backdated to 14 September.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
sentences.text: The President is therefore not required to consult the Council of Presidential Advisers and is not subject to any time limit in deciding whether to take up an international appointment under the Article.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
sentences.text: I should also mention that, out of an abundance of caution, we have backdated the new Article 22Q to 14 September, when President Tharman assumed office.

sections.label: Cabinet advice on President's roles
sections.summary: If the Bill passes, Cabinet intends to advise the President to continue existing international roles in his private capacity, effective forward-looking.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
sentences.text: Should the Bill be passed by Parliament, Cabinet intends to advise the President that it is in the national interest for the President to continue in his existing international roles in his private capacity, and this will take effect on a forward-looking basis.

sections.label: Ministers' foreign roles framework
sections.summary: The framework resembles Article 22Q but Ministers need the Prime Minister's permission and instructions; Article 33A supersedes the Ministerial Code, and Senior Minister Teo may continue his TotalEnergies appointment.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
sentences.text: The framework is similar to Article 22Q, except that Ministers must obtain the permission of the Prime Minister and are subject to his instructions.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong) (for the Prime Minister)
sentences.text: The new Article 33A will supersede the relevant portions of the Ministerial Code, and the Prime Minister intends to give permission to Senior Minister Teo to continue with his TotalEnergies appointment under the new framework.

sections.label: Bill purpose for foreign roles
sections.summary: The Bill amends the Constitution to let the President and Cabinet Ministers take roles in foreign and international organisations privately when it serves the national interest.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: The purpose of this Bill is to amend the Constitution to enable Singapore's President and Cabinet Ministers to assume roles in foreign and international organisations in their private capacity, when it serves the national interest.

sections.label: Framework for President and Ministers
sections.summary: Article 22Q clause 2 sets conditions for the President's foreign office, clause 3 applies the same framework to Ministers, creating transparency, accountability and governance.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: In the case of the President, clause 2 in Article 22Q of the Bill spells out the conditions under which the President can accept and hold office in a foreign or international organisation, in his private capacity.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Clause 3 similarly inserts provisions to apply the same framework to Ministers and empowers the Prime Minister to approve such appointments.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: The new provisions of both the clauses create a formal framework to ensure greater transparency, accountability and governance when the President and Cabinet Ministers perform non-local roles in their private capacities.

sections.label: MP's concerns and conclusion
sections.summary: The Bill lacks clarity on the Prime Minister's situation and may involve extra expenditure, but the speaker concludes its benefits outweigh the concerns.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: The Bill currently outlines advice mechanisms for the President and Cabinet Ministers, but lacks clarity regarding the Prime Minister's situation.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Although it is stated that the Bill will not involve the Government in any extra financial expenditure, it may not be so, in reality.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: In cases involving national interest spaces like the economy, security, human development and healthcare, the Government's provision of such support should be considered.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: There will be times when it is essential to help ensure the organised conduct of the businesses, to ensure that the status of the President and Cabinet Ministers are at least retained for the image of Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Therefore, in conclusion, I believe that the benefits of this Bill outweigh the concerns.

sections.label: President's international appointments listed
sections.summary: President Tharman holds international appointments including G30 Chairman, UNHDR Co-chair, GCEW Co-chair and WEF Board of Trustees member.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: President Tharman Shanmugaratnam currently holds several international appointments, including Chairman of the Board of Trustees of the G30, Co-chair of the advisory board of the UN Human Development Report (UNHDR), Co-chair of the Global Commission on the Economics of Water (GCEW) and a member of the Board of Trustees of the World Economic Forum (WEF).

sections.label: President's salary and office expenditure
sections.summary: The President draws a $1.57 million yearly salary, and his office's budgeted expenditure this financial year exceeds $12 million.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The President also draws a salary of $1.57 million a year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: If we include his entertainment allowance, the salaries of his personal staff and other expenses, the total budgeted expenditure of the President's office in the current financial year is over $12 million.

sections.label: Article 22Q private capacity
sections.summary: The proposed Article 22Q specifies the President will act in his private capacity, not in exercise of his constitutional functions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Government may argue that the President serves Singapore by accepting these key positions in international organisations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: However, we must note that the proposed Article 22Q specifies that he will act in his “private capacity”, not in the exercise of his functions under the Constitution.

sections.label: Workers' Party opposes the Bill
sections.summary: The Workers' Party will vote against the Bill, saying external appointments in private capacity could detract from the President's public duties.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Is there any objective test that the Cabinet will employ to assess the degree of national interest of the President taking up foreign or international roles?

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Allowing the President to take up external appointments in his private capacity could detract from his substantial public duties.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: For this reason, the Workers' Party (WP) will vote against this Bill.

sections.label: Limits on Ministers' private appointments
sections.summary: The passage asks whether the Government will limit the numbers and type of appointments Ministers can take on in their private capacities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Will the Government limit the numbers and type of appointments Ministers can take on in their private capacities?

sections.label: Cabinet screening and support for Bill
sections.summary: The passage asks how the Cabinet would screen and vet invitations, calls for conflict-of-interest mechanics, and expresses full support for the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: How would the Cabinet screen, vet and make recommendations for appropriate invitations to be approved?

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: We must also put in place mechanics to prevent conflict of interest for the President and Ministers with such appointments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: I am in full support of the Bill because for Singapore, one of the smallest nations in the world, having our Ministers or President on select, curated international organisations, will allow us to put our views across and have a say in how certain future international rules will be designed.

sections.label: Backdating constitutional amendments to inauguration
sections.summary: Parliament is asked to backdate the constitutional amendments to 14 September 2023, President Tharman's inauguration date, creating unease among Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Parliament is also being asked to backdate these proposed constitutional amendments to 14 September 2023, the date of President Tharman's inauguration, through clause 1(2) of this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The speed with which these constitutional amendments are being enacted, as well as the fact that they are being backdated, have created unnecessary unease among Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: A segment of Singaporeans now perceives that the Constitution is being specially amended to enable President Tharman to continue serving in international organisations despite taking up his new office as President of Singapore.

sections.label: Article 22Q and President's appointments
sections.summary: The Bill introduces Article 22Q allowing the President to hold foreign and international offices if the Cabinet advises it is in the national interest and the President concurs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: If there is a possibility that President Tharman's foreign and international appointments are unconstitutional, then what this House is doing today creates a worrying precedent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: This House is being asked to change the highest law in the land and backdate the change to enable a specific individual to remain within legal boundaries.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: From the feedback we have gathered, there is confusion on the ground and Singaporeans need a full explanation from the Government.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: Under the proposed Article 22Q which is being introduced by this amendment Bill, the President may accept and hold an office in a foreign and international organisation in his private capacity if, and only if, the President is not disabled by Article 19A(1) from performing the functions of that office; the Cabinet advises the President that it is in the national interest for the President to accept and hold that office; and the President, acting in his discretion, concurs with the advice of the Cabinet.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: The PMO said in a statement that, from time to time, the President or Ministers are invited to take up key positions in foreign and international organisations, and I quote: "Accepting such positions can enhance Singapore’s international standing and help to advance our national interest..." It has already been reported in The Straits Times that if the Bill is passed, it would allow President Tharman to continue with his roles in the WEF and G30.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: We are told that President Tharman currently holds several international appointments, including being chairman of the Board of Trustees of the G30, a member of the WEF’s Board of Trustees, Co-chair of the GCEW, and Co-chair of the Advisory Board for the UN Human Development Report (UNHDR).

sections.label: Safeguards in the amendment Bill
sections.summary: The Government argues the Bill has safeguards, including Cabinet advice on national interest and Cabinet power to require relinquishment under Article 22Q.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: The Government has argued that it has safeguards built into this amendment Bill, for example, under Article 22Q(1), the Cabinet must be able to advise the President that it is in the national interest for the President to accept and hold that office and, under Article 22Q(2), the Cabinet may, from time to time, advise the President against saying something or doing anything in the performance of the functions of any new office that the President is holding privately and the Cabinet may require the President to relinquish his responsibility under Article 22Q(3).

sections.label: Conflicts from double-hatting
sections.summary: Conflicts of interest may happen when one is double-hatting.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: Conflicts of interest may happen when one is double-hatting.

sections.label: No accountability beyond relinquishment
sections.summary: The Bill provides for the President to relinquish an external position when asked, but does not provide for how the President can be held accountable.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: Beyond Article 22Q(2) providing for the Cabinet to advise the President against saying or doing anything in his capacity as appointment holder of such a foreign or international organisation, the Cabinet can ask the President to relinquish the external position he is holding pursuant to Article 22Q(3) and, under this provision, he must so relinquish, when asked.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: However, beyond relinquishing, the Bill, significantly, does not provide for how the President can be held accountable when such a situation happens.

sections.label: No taxpayer monies for private appointments
sections.summary: The Bill does not expressly allow taxpayers' monies to be spent on the examples mentioned, especially as these appointments are held in a private capacity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: The Bill, as it stands, does not expressly allow taxpayers’ monies to be spent in the examples I have mentioned, especially as these appointments are held in a private capacity.

sections.label: WP vote against Bill
sections.summary: The WP will vote against this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
sentences.text: The WP will, therefore, vote against this Bill.

sections.label: President and Ministers conflict of interest
sections.summary: It asks how the offices of the President and Ministers would manage potential conflict of interest from appointments in their personal capacities and how input at these bodies will be in the national interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: How would the offices of the President and Ministers manage potential conflict of interest which may arise due to the appointment in their personal capacities?

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: How can we be assured that all input by our President and Ministers at these bodies will be in our national interest?

sections.label: Fees, expenses and support for Bill
sections.summary: It raises questions about to whom or which office fees, honorariums, and expenses such as travel, security detail and accommodation will be paid, but concludes with support for the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Other questions which arise are about to whom or which office will be paid the fees and honorariums from the organisations and the billing of expenses, such as travel, security detail and accommodation, if any.

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Despite these concerns, I would like to conclude with my support for the Bill in view of the benefits and glory such appointments will bring to Singapore.

sections.label: Retroactive Bills in Hansard
sections.summary: A Hansard search for "deemed to have come into operation" found few Bills with retroactive applicability, one being the Republic of Singapore Independence Act, raised in December 1965 but commenced on 9 August.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Based on a search in Hansard for the term "deemed to have come into operation", I was able to identify only a handful of other instances of Bills where retroactive applicability was hardcoded into the language of the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: One is the Republic of Singapore Independence Act (RSIA), which was raised for First and Second Readings only in December 1965 but commenced on Singapore Day, 9 August, for obvious reasons.

sections.label: Retroactivity justification and constitutional articles
sections.summary: It states retroactivity has always been heavily justified, should be sparing, and that the Bill does not contravene Articles 9 or 11 of the Constitution.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In 1992, proposed changes to the mandatory death penalty for homicide offences were also applied to existing cases.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: But, importantly, as far as I can gather, the common thread among these instances is that the case for retroactivity was always heavily justified, based on the importance of implications that could result were the law not applied retroactively – and it has never been applied to any constitutional amendment since 2007.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: I believe Members of this House will, therefore, agree with me that all instances where retroactive legislation making is enacted to be sparing and any such cases should be justifiable by the gravity of otherwise not doing so.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: To be clear, I am not suggesting that there is any incoherence between the Bill at hand and our Constitution itself since the right to due process implied by Article 9 of the Constitution pertains to life and liberty, neither of which are threatened with compromise by the proposed amendments, nor does the present Bill appear to be in contravention to Article 11, which offers protection against retrospective criminal laws.

sections.label: Government awareness of constitutional conflict
sections.summary: It asks whether the Government treated the matter lightly and when it first became aware of a possible conflict with the Constitution necessitating a potential amendment.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Or has the Government itself treated the matter lightly, taking for granted the fact that, with a supermajority in Parliament, it is able to alter the Constitution at will and, hence, it would simply be a fait accompli to roll out a retroactive amendment?

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: It would be useful for this House to know when the Government was first made aware of a possible conflict with the Constitution which would necessitate a potential amendment.

sections.label: Retroactive lawmaking for private positions
sections.summary: The passage asks whether retroactively allowing the President and Ministers to take private positions justifies departing from prospective lawmaking, and states WP cannot support the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Does this House regard the use of retroactive lawmaking embodied in this Bill – that we should retrospectively allow the President and Ministers to take on positions in their private capacity should it serve the national interest – as one that is sufficiently grave as to justify bending away from the sound, general principles of prospective lawmaking?

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: For me, it is closer to the latter and, for that reason, I and the WP cannot support the Bill.

sections.label: SIF and UN SDGs engagement
sections.summary: The passage describes SIF initiatives, the Young Social Entrepreneurs Programme, the UN SDGs, and hopes for a whole-of-society approach to global engagement.

sentences.speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Since 1991, SIF has brought together communities in a variety of initiatives with the aim to connect and collaborate for positive change.

sentences.speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: One programme, the Young Social Entrepreneurs Programme, brings together social entrepreneurs from the region each year to sharpen their socially driven initiatives, undergo mentoring and, eventually, participate in a final pitching session.

sentences.speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are currently behind schedule and many are unlikely to achieve the targets set for 2030.

sentences.speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The SDGs have attracted both public and private funding and have been often used to benchmark philanthropic giving across all levels.

sentences.speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: While we may not specifically align our various public and private philanthropic endeavours with the UN SDGs, we are, nevertheless, engaging in many of these goals through many ongoing public programmes and private and people initiatives.

sentences.speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I hope that as our leaders engage at the highest levels, there will be consideration for building a whole-of-society approach to global engagement.

sentences.speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Working with young and aspiring leaders and also, in particular, social entrepreneurs, they have much to offer to the Singapore of today and tomorrow.

sections.label: Bill allows private capacity office
sections.summary: The passage states the Bill seeks to allow the President or Ministers to hold and accept office in their private capacity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, the Bill seeks to allow the President or Ministers to hold and accept office in their "private capacity".

sections.label: Foreign roles and national interests
sections.summary: The passage states the role of the President and Ministers in foreign organisations must not run counter to national interests.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Second, Mr Speaker, Sir, the role of the President and Ministers in foreign organisations must not run counter to our national interests.

sections.label: Moratorium on foreign organisation service
sections.summary: The passage asks whether a moratorium exists on a transferred Minister's service in a foreign organisation that could pose a conflict of interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: In addition, if a Minister had served, for instance, in the Ministry of National Development but is now transferred to another portfolio, is there a moratorium on their service in a foreign organisation that could pose a conflict of interest?

sections.label: External commitments and remuneration
sections.summary: The passage states leaders must not become entangled in external commitments to the detriment of national duties, and remuneration for external positions must be addressed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: We must prevent a scenario where our leaders become entangled in external commitments to the detriment of their duties to the nation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: We must address the issue of remuneration for these external positions.

sections.label: President foreign office conditions
sections.summary: Proposed Article 22Q lets the President accept a foreign or international office in his private capacity, subject to Cabinet advice and limits.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: The proposed Article 22Q allows the President to accept and hold an office in a foreign or international organisation in his private capacity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: This, of course, is limited by Article 19A(1), meaning that he cannot actively engage in any commercial enterprise.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: The President can only accept such a role if the Cabinet advises him that it is for the national interests and he himself concurs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Furthermore, even after the acceptance of such a role, the President is limited against saying or doing anything in that role if the Cabinet so advises, and must relinquish the role if so advised by the Cabinet.

sections.label: Organisations wanting President's personal views
sections.summary: Organisations wanted the President's personal views, unfettered by the government, so Articles 22 to 22Q set conditions on what he can do.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: We could have easily carried on the status quo of having the President carry out duties in his official capacity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: But as I understand it and as I understand Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong's speech, it was the organisations who said, "Yes, you have brought forth an even greater ballast by your elevation to Head of State, and brings with the credibility to the organisation, but actually what we really want are your personal views, so you are not fettered by what the government of the day thinks." And that presented a novel situation, which, in good conscience, the Attorney-General flagged out, and which we are ironing out today.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: It is honest and transparent Parliamentary business that we are passing today.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: And if, indeed, there are any disagreements, which I think Mr Leong, or maybe another Member alluded to, that is exactly why we have Article 22 to Article 22Q, which places in conditions what the President can do and cannot do.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: And the last limb, if I am not mistaken, if the Cabinet is of the view that the President does not carry on these duties, he must relinquish them.

sections.label: Elected President and Article 11
sections.summary: The elected President gives Singapore both, and Article 11 concerns criminal offences, so it is not relevant to this debate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In the President, in who is elected, we can actually have both, and what a fillip advantage that would be for Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim then speaks about retroactivity, and I think when I listened very carefully, the hon Member talked about some element of retrospectivity and raised Article 11.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: I do not have Article 11 with me here now, but Article 11 actually talks about criminal offences.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: And therefore, it is not, strictly speaking, relevant to what we are debating today.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: So, what we are doing today is not incoherent with the Constitution.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: But we do not." I would like to take that conclusion and flip it on its head.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: I am humbly proud, that I am part of the two-thirds that pushes through constitutional legislations that are robustly in favour of our national interests.

sections.label: Three conditions for President
sections.summary: Three conditions must be met: the President must be disabled by article 19A(1), the Cabinet must advise national interest, and the President must concur.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Three conditions must be met before the President may do so.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: First, the President must be disabled by article 19A(1) from performing the function of the office.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Second, the Cabinet must advise the President that it is in the national interest for the President to accept and hold the office.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
sentences.text: Third, the President acting in his discretion must concur with the Cabinet's advice.

sections.label: Official versus private capacity appointments
sections.summary: The Member supports the WP position on official capacity appointments and asks whether this Bill first differentiates official and private capacity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: I am totally in support of the WP's position, explained by Member Gerald Giam.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: We are in support of the official capacity if our Ministers perform the international appointments in their official capacities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: Our Ministers have, in the past, been always taking up all these international appointments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: Is it the first time, through this Bill, that we are differentiating official capacity and private capacity?

sections.label: No Prime Ministers in organisations
sections.summary: The Government does not intend for current or future Prime Ministers to serve in international organisations.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: In my opening remarks, I said we do not intend, the Government does not intend for either the current or future Prime Ministers to serve in international organisations.

sections.label: Caution on President's foreign roles
sections.summary: The provision will not be used and the President's appointment approval will be prospective, with foreign roles allowed only in private capacity if in the national interest.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: But in any case, setting aside the principle of it as I had highlighted just now, we are doing this out of an abundance of caution.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We will not use this provision, and the approval of the President's appointment will be done on a prospective basis.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: The framework that we are setting out makes it clear that the President or the Minister, can only hold a foreign or international role in their private capacities, if it is in the national interest to do so.

sections.label: Safeguard on commenting
sections.summary: Safeguards mean the President is not able to comment on domestic policies and politics.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Safeguards are not so much that we control what he says, but we say that he is not able to comment on domestic policies and politics.

sections.label: Framework for grey zone
sections.summary: The Government chose to be upfront and pass a proper framework in Parliament rather than operate with ambiguity.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: He will essentially be operating in a new, novel and grey zone.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: And that is why the Government decided it is far better to be upfront, transparent and direct about this matter instead of operating in an area with some ambiguity.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We come to Parliament, pass a proper and principled framework and work within this framework going forward.

sections.label: Government foots President's costs
sections.summary: The Government foots the Bill for the President's trips, which are on Cabinet advice and in the national interest.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: In fact, while some of the international organisations, the ones I cited, would be willing to pay for the President's cost, we think it is proper that the Government foots the Bill because when we do this, when the President goes on these trips, as I said, it is on the advice of the Cabinet and it is in the national interest that he holds these national appointments.

sections.label: Conflict and no commitments
sections.summary: Appointments conflicting with official functions are not in Singapore's national interest, and the President and Ministers cannot make commitments for the Government.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Clearly, it would not be in Singapore’s national interest to support appointments that place the President or a Minister in conflict with their official functions.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: And furthermore, as I explained in my opening remarks, the President and Ministers will not be able to make any commitments on behalf of the Government of Singapore in the course of such engagements in international bodies.

sections.label: No remuneration retention
sections.summary: The President and Ministers may not retain remuneration or benefits from private-capacity appointments, and the President has received none.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: On the issue of remuneration, I confirm that that the President and Ministers may not retain any remuneration or benefits in connection with appointments in their private capacity.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: The President has not received any such remuneration or other benefits, like an honorarium from the international bodies that he is represented on currently.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: And should he be offered such benefits, the President is expected to decline it or to donate the sum to charity.

sections.label: President Tharman international bodies attendance
sections.summary: President Tharman has not attended any formal meetings of the four international bodies he was appointed to since 14 September.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Up to now, out of an abundance of caution, I should say, President Tharman has not attended any formal meetings of the four international bodies that he has been appointed to since 14 September and prior to this reading in Parliament.

sections.label: Cabinet agrees President continuing roles
sections.summary: Cabinet agreed to the President continuing in these roles, and the Constitution is being amended so he can act independently while a framework protects his constitutional duties.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: And Cabinet has readily agreed to President continuing in these roles because they bring credit to Singapore, underline our usefulness to the world and project our influence abroad effectively.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: And so, we are amending the Constitution so that the President can act independently to bring value to the organisations he operates in, while serving our national interest, because he is the Head of State, and this is why it is novel.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Previously, it was okay for Ministers, but now we are dealing with the President.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: It is a new situation and because he is the Head of State, we have put in place a framework to ensure his participation in these international bodies does not affect in any way his constitutional responsibilities to Singaporeans or the discharge of his custodial duties.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: The President will not be directly representing Singapore's official positions in these bodies or commenting on any of Singapore's domestic or foreign policies abroad.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: And when there is any danger of him being put in a difficult position or in conflict with national interest, the Cabinet will advise him not to take part or even to withdraw from the body.

sections.label: AGC advice on Constitution
sections.summary: The AGC has advised this is an area that the Constitution does not clearly provide for.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: The AGC has advised this is an area that the Constitution does not clearly provide for.

sections.label: Second Reading voting results
sections.summary: The Second Reading was carried with 75 Ayes, eight Noes and zero Abstentions, by not less than two-thirds of Elected and Non-Constituency Members.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: I will proceed to declare the voting results now.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: There are 75 "Ayes"; eight "Noes"; and zero "Abstentions".

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: The Second Reading of the Bill has been carried by the votes of not less than two-thirds of the total number of Elected and Non-Constituency Members of Parliament.

sections.label: Third Reading voting result
sections.summary: The Third Reading was carried by the votes of not less than two-thirds of the total number of Elected and Non-Constituency Members of Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: The Third Reading of the Bill has been carried by the votes of not less than two-thirds of the total number of Elected and Non-Constituency Members of Parliament.
